lines.text: Along the Nile, the kingdom of Kush built pyramids, a Mahdi drove out an empire, and a modern nation has fought to find peace. This is the story of Sudan.
Everything here follows the Nile, the great river of north-east Africa, which has carved its path for millions of years.
Around 1070 BCE, the Nubian kingdom of Kush rose on the upper Nile. Its kings would even rule Egypt as pharaohs for a time.
Later its capital moved south to Meroe, where the kings were buried under steep pyramids and iron was worked on a great scale.
After Kush faded, Christian kingdoms ruled the Nile. Makuria was the strongest, and it lasted almost a thousand years.
In the early 1500s, Sennar rose on the Blue Nile as the seat of a new power.
It was the capital of the Funj Sultanate, which ruled the land for three centuries.
In 1821, Egypt conquered Sudan, and Khartoum grew where the White and Blue Nile meet, to become the capital.
Muhammad Ahmad, a religious leader born in 1844, declared himself the Mahdi and rallied Sudanese against Egyptian rule.
His forces besieged Khartoum for nearly a year. In January 1885 the city fell, and the British general Gordon was killed.
In 1898, at Omdurman, British and Egyptian forces with modern guns crushed the Mahdist army.
Britain and Egypt then ruled Sudan jointly, though in practice it was the British who governed, for more than half a century.
Omar al-Bashir, born in 1944, would seize power as a soldier and rule Sudan for thirty years.
On the first of January 1956, Sudan became independent. But peace between its north and south would prove hard to find.
In 1983, war between the north and the south broke out again. It lasted more than twenty years, one of the deadliest of the century.
In 2003, war broke out in Darfur, in the far west, bringing terrible suffering to its people.
That same year, work began on the Merowe Dam, a great barrier across the Nile finished in 2009.
In 2011, after decades of war, the south voted to leave, and South Sudan became a country of its own.
Two years later the Rapid Support Forces were formed, a paramilitary force grown from the Janjaweed militias of Darfur.
In December 2018, Sudanese filled the streets. Months of protest ended al-Bashir's rule in 2019.
But hope gave way in 2023, when the army and the Rapid Support Forces turned their guns on each other, and war returned.
From the pyramids of Meroe to a land at war once more, Sudan's people still wait for lasting peace.
